title: curl, Postman, and OpenAPI
summary: Use the API the way its callers do with curl, Postman, and code, describe it in an OpenAPI document, and change it without breaking clients.
intro: So far you've built Roombook from the inside: routes, rules, tables, and logins. The people who use it never see any of that. A student's phone app, a door display, and a teammate's script see only requests and responses, and what your documentation says about them. This lesson takes the caller's side. You'll call the API the way callers do, with curl in the terminal, with Postman, and from Spring Boot code. Then you'll describe the whole API in an OpenAPI document, the machine-readable contract that docs pages, client generators, and test tools all read, and see how Spring Boot produces one. It ends with how to change an API that people already depend on without breaking them.

steps.title: The API from the caller's side
steps.body:
Your callers can't read your code, and they shouldn't have to. Everything they know about Roombook comes from the requests they send, the answers they get, and what your documentation says. An API that's pleasant from the outside gets used, and gets fewer support questions. One that's confusing from the outside is a bad API, however clean the inside is.

## What a caller needs

- **Predictable answers.** Every endpoint follows the same rules: JSON fields in camelCase, times in RFC 3339 in UTC, lists as `{"items": [...], "nextCursor": ...}`, and every error as Problem Details. Learn one endpoint and you can guess the rest.
- **The first five minutes.** Someone new wants one successful call, fast: the base URL, how to get a token, and one example to copy. If that takes an afternoon, they pick another API, or they message you.
- **Errors that say what to fix.** A bare 400 starts a guessing game. A Problem Details body that names each bad field and why ends it, as the first example below shows.
- **Documentation, and help in their own language.** Docs list every endpoint with its inputs and outputs. Many APIs also ship an **SDK**, a software development kit: a library in the caller's language that wraps each HTTP call in a function, so `roombook.getRoom(2)` replaces building a request by hand.
- **A changelog.** A dated list of what changed in each release, so callers learn about a new field or a removed one before it surprises them.

## Three ways to call an API

An **HTTP client** is any program that sends HTTP requests and reads the responses. Your browser is one. Three more come up every week when you work on an API:

- **curl**, in the terminal: quick to type, easy to paste into a bug report, and on every computer. The next part goes through the flags APIs need.
- **Postman**, a desktop app for saving requests and sharing them with a team, covered after curl.
- **Code**, when another program needs the API: a script, another service, a test. Every language has an HTTP client for this.

```diagram clients-and-openapi-three-clients
Three clients, one request: the server can't tell them apart.
```

They all send the same thing: a request line, headers, and a body, over a connection to the server's port. Roombook can't tell which one called, except by the `User-Agent` header each one sends with its name. So anything you can do in one, you can do in the others, and a request that fails in your code fails the same way in curl, where it's easier to look at.

## Calling Roombook from Spring Boot

Spring's HTTP client is **RestClient**, part of Spring Framework since 6.1, so it's already in your project with the web starter. You build one with a base URL and chain calls: the method, the URI, then `retrieve()` and `body(Type.class)`, which turns the JSON into a record with the same Jackson that writes your responses. Unlike most clients, `retrieve()` throws on an error status: an `HttpClientErrorException` for a 4xx and an `HttpServerErrorException` for a 5xx. You set timeouts on the request factory underneath it, since by default it would wait a very long time. The reliability lesson sets them for every client Spring Boot builds.

The second and third examples show a small program in `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/tools/ShowRoom.java` that reads one room, and what it prints when the room doesn't exist.

examples.title: An error that says what to fix
examples.prompt: Ask for a token with a bad email and no password. `-s` hides curl's progress meter, and `| jq` prints the JSON with indentation, which the next part explains.
examples.explanation: The status is 422, Validation failed, and the body says exactly what to change: the email isn't an email address, and the password is missing. Both come back at once, so the caller fixes everything in one go, instead of finding one problem per request. `instance` is the path that failed, and `requestId` matches the `X-Request-Id` header on the response. A caller who quotes it in a bug report lets you find that exact request in your logs. This is what "errors as documentation" means: someone who has never read your docs can still fix the request.

examples.title: Reading one room from code
examples.prompt: `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/tools/ShowRoom.java`, a small program that reads one room and prints it. Run it with Roombook running on port 8080, with the room's id as an argument.
examples.explanation: This is a plain `main` method, not a Spring app: `spring-boot:run` with `main-class` just runs it with the project's classpath, which already has RestClient and Jackson. The record `Room` lists the fields the script needs, and Jackson fills them from the JSON. `setReadTimeout` makes a call fail after five seconds instead of waiting. `retrieve()` throws `HttpClientErrorException` on the 404, and `getResponseBodyAs(ProblemDetail.class)` reads the body as the same Problem Details type your controllers send. Inside a Spring service you'd make the `RestClient` a bean, built once from the injected `RestClient.Builder`, instead of in `main`.

examples.title: When the answer is an error
examples.prompt: Run it for room 99, which doesn't exist, and then for room 2.
examples.explanation: Room 99 gets a 404, and the program prints the problem's status and title, `Resource not found`, from the body. Room 2 prints its line. Most of the work in a real client is this second path: deciding what each error means for your program. A 404 here means a wrong id. A 401 means sign in again. A 429 or a 503 means wait and retry, which the reliability lesson covers. Printing the title, and keeping the request id, makes a failure easy to report.
examples.output:
Failed: 404 Resource not found
Lovelace in main-library seats 4: whiteboard

steps.title: curl in depth
steps.body:
curl is the one client you'll find everywhere: on every server you log into, in nearly every API's documentation, and in bug reports, where "here's the curl that fails" saves an hour of back and forth. When the web app shows a vague error, curl shows you exactly what the server said. The web course used it to read requests with `-i`, `-v`, and `-I`. APIs need a few more flags.

## The flags you'll use

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `-i` | Prints the status line and headers before the body |
| `-v` | Prints everything sent and received, for debugging |
| `-X PATCH` | Sets the method. A body alone means POST, so you need it for PUT, PATCH, and DELETE |
| `-H "Name: value"` | Adds a header, like `Authorization` |
| `--json '...'` | Sends a JSON body, with `Content-Type` and `Accept` set to `application/json` |
| `-d '...'` | Sends a body as a form, with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` |
| `--json @file` | Reads the body from a file, and `-d @file` does the same |
| `-c file`, `-b file` | Saves the cookies the server sets, and sends them back |
| `-s`, `-S` | Hides the progress meter, and still shows errors |
| `-o file` | Writes the body to a file, so `-o /dev/null` throws it away |
| `-w '...'` | Prints facts when the request is done, like `%{http_code}` or `%{time_total}` |
| `--fail-with-body` | Exits with an error code on a 4xx or 5xx, and still prints the body |

The `-d` row is a classic trap. `curl -d '{"roomId": 1}'` sends JSON text labeled as a form, and an API that checks `Content-Type` answers 415 Unsupported Media Type, or worse, tries to read it as a form. Use `--json`, which arrived in curl 7.82 in 2022, or add `-H "Content-Type: application/json"` yourself.

`-c` and `-b` are how curl acts like a browser for a cookie session. Logging in with `-c cookies.txt` saves the `Set-Cookie` from the answer to a file, and each later request with `-b cookies.txt` sends it back, the way the authentication lesson's session login expects. The scaling lesson uses exactly this.

## jq, and keeping a token

**jq**, which the authentication lesson used to read a token, is a small command-line program that reads JSON and picks pieces out of it. `jq` alone prints it with indentation, `jq -r .accessToken` prints one field as plain text, and `jq '.items[].name'` prints every room's name. It isn't part of curl: install it with `brew install jq` on a Mac, `sudo apt install jq` on Debian or Ubuntu, or `winget install jqlang.jq` on Windows.

Together with a shell variable, jq turns signing in into one line. `TOKEN=$(...)` runs the command inside and keeps what it prints, so every later request can send `Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN`. Keep the request body in a file too, `booking.json`, so you don't fight the shell's quoting:

```json
{
  "roomId": 1,
  "startsAt": "2026-10-05T14:00:00Z",
  "endsAt": "2026-10-05T15:30:00Z",
  "attendees": 3,
  "note": "Algorithms study group"
}
```

The examples below walk through signing in, booking that room, and booking it again. A few more shapes are worth knowing. jq can format each item of a list as text, and `-w` with `-o /dev/null` prints just the status and the time a request took, which is handy in a quick loop:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/v1/rooms | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.id)  \(.name)  \(.capacity) seats"'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' http://localhost:8080/v1/rooms
```

```text
1  Turing  6 seats
2  Lovelace  4 seats
3  Hopper  8 seats
200 in 0.002322s
```

## Requests in a file

A `requests.http` file keeps requests next to the code, in plain text that VS Code's REST Client extension and JetBrains IDEs send with one click. `###` separates requests, `@name = value` sets a variable, and `{{name}}` uses it:

```http
@base = http://localhost:8080
@token = paste-an-access-token-here

### Book Turing on Monday
POST {{base}}/v1/bookings
Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
Content-Type: application/json

{"roomId": 1, "startsAt": "2026-10-05T14:00:00Z", "endsAt": "2026-10-05T15:30:00Z", "attendees": 3}
```

Commit it, and the next person on the project gets working examples on day one, which beats a list of commands in someone's shell history.

examples.title: Signing in and keeping the token
examples.prompt: With Roombook running on port 8080, the first command shows the token response. The second keeps just the token in `TOKEN` and prints nothing.
examples.code:
curl -s --json '{"email": "ada@roombook.example", "password": "correct horse battery staple"}' http://localhost:8080/v1/auth/token | jq
TOKEN=$(curl -s --json '{"email": "ada@roombook.example", "password": "correct horse battery staple"}' http://localhost:8080/v1/auth/token | jq -r .accessToken)
examples.explanation: `--json` sent the body as JSON and the method as POST, since a body without `-X` means POST. The answer is the token pair from the authentication lesson: the access token, a JWT, with its type and its lifetime in seconds, 900 being 15 minutes, and the refresh token that gets a new pair when the access token runs out. The second command runs the same request, and `jq -r .accessToken` prints only the token, without quotes, so the shell stores the bare string. Never paste a real token into a bug report or a chat: anyone holding it is Ada until it expires.

examples.title: Booking a room from the terminal
examples.prompt: Send `booking.json` with the token. `-i` shows the status line and headers.
examples.explanation: `201 Created` with a `Location` header is the answer the routes lesson promised for a POST that makes something: the new booking lives at `/v1/bookings/1001`, and the body is the booking itself. `X-Request-Id` is the id the middleware lesson added to every response. The `createdAt` is the database's own clock, since PostgreSQL fills it in with `now()`, so yours shows the moment you ran it. The status line has no reason phrase after 201: Tomcat stopped sending them, since HTTP/1.1 allows it and clients only read the number.

examples.title: The same booking again, the way a script sees it
examples.prompt: Run the same request again. `--fail-with-body` makes curl fail on a 4xx or 5xx, and `echo $?` prints the exit code curl left behind.
examples.explanation: The room is taken now, so the answer is 409, Room already booked, as a problem. `--fail-with-body` did two things: curl printed its own error line, `(22)`, and exited with code 22 instead of 0, so a script stops right there, if it runs with `set -e`, the shell setting that ends a script at the first failed command. So does a **CI** job, short for continuous integration: a computer that builds and checks the code on every push. Without the flag, curl exits 0 for any answer at all, even a 500, since from its side the request worked. Plain `--fail` also fails but throws the body away, and the body is the part that says why. `-w '\n'` only adds a line break after the body.

steps.title: Postman
steps.body:
curl is perfect for one request. A team working on an API needs more: a shared, organized set of requests that anyone can open and send, with the URLs and tokens filled in. **Postman** is the most widely used tool for that, a desktop and web app for building, saving, and sharing HTTP requests, free for small teams. Postman is a company's product, and it keeps your saved work in its cloud. That's convenient, and it means you think about what you put in it.

## Collections

A **collection** is a named set of saved requests, grouped in folders. Each saved request keeps its method, URL, headers, body, and scripts. A Roombook collection mirrors the API:

```text
Roombook
├── Auth
│   └── Sign in            POST {{baseUrl}}/v1/auth/token
├── Rooms
│   ├── List rooms         GET  {{baseUrl}}/v1/rooms
│   └── Get a room         GET  {{baseUrl}}/v1/rooms/{{roomId}}
└── Bookings
    ├── Book a room        POST {{baseUrl}}/v1/bookings
    └── Get a booking      GET  {{baseUrl}}/v1/bookings/{{bookingId}}
```

You don't have to type it. Postman can import an OpenAPI document, which the next part introduces, and build the whole collection from it, one request per operation, with example bodies filled in.

## Environments and variables

`{{baseUrl}}` is a **variable**: Postman swaps in its value when it sends the request. An **environment** is a named set of values for those variables, and you pick one from a menu at the top. A Local environment sets `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:8080`, and a Staging one points at a test server, so the same collection works against both. Variables also live in the collection itself, for values every environment shares, like `roomId`.

Keep secrets out of anything shared. Collections and environments sync to Postman's servers and to everyone in the workspace, so a real password or token saved there is a leaked password. Mark sensitive variables as secret, keep their real values only on your own computer or in Postman's vault, which stores secrets locally and never syncs them, and use throwaway test accounts. A token that a script fetches at run time, as below, never needs saving at all.

## Auth, and scripts

The **Authorization** tab of a request, or of the whole collection, handles credentials for you: choose Bearer Token and enter `{{accessToken}}`, and Postman adds the header to every request. Other types cover API keys, basic auth, and the OAuth 2 flows from the lesson on API keys and OAuth.

Each request can also run **scripts**, short JavaScript that Postman runs on its side: a pre-request script before sending, and a post-response script after the answer arrives. Postman gives them an object called `pm`. `pm.response` is the answer, `pm.environment.set()` saves a variable, and `pm.test()` names a check that shows as passed or failed. Checks use `pm.expect`, from a library called Chai, which reads like a sentence: `pm.expect(booking.status).to.eql("confirmed")`. The examples below sign in and save the token, then check the booking request. Send them in order, and every request after Sign in is authenticated.

## Running a whole collection

The **Collection Runner** sends every request in a collection, in order, and shows each test's result, which is a quick check after a change. The **Postman CLI** does the same from a terminal, so a CI job can run it too, as the next lesson shows. It exits with an error code when any test fails, so the build fails with it:

```bash
postman login --with-api-key "$POSTMAN_API_KEY"
postman collection run <collection-id> -e <environment-id>
```

`<collection-id>` and `<environment-id>` come from the collection's and environment's Info panels in Postman, and the API key from your account settings, stored in the CI system's secrets. Other tools do the same job, and some keep collections as plain files in your repository instead of a cloud workspace. Bruno and Insomnia are two you'll hear about.

examples.title: A sign-in request that saves the token
examples.prompt: The post-response script on the Sign in request, which sends Ada's email and password. It runs after each answer arrives.
examples.explanation: `pm.test` names a check, and Postman lists it under Test Results with a pass or a fail. Inside, `pm.response.to.have.status(200)` fails the test on any other status, `pm.response.json()` reads the body, and `pm.environment.set` stores the token in the current environment, where `{{accessToken}}` picks it up. The token lives only as long as the environment's local value, and expires in 15 minutes anyway, so send Sign in again when requests start getting 401.

examples.title: Tests on the booking request
examples.prompt: The post-response script on Book a room, which sends the booking JSON with the Bearer Token auth from the collection.
examples.explanation: The first test checks the contract from the routes lesson: 201, a `Location` that points at the new booking, and a body with the right status and start time. It saves the new id in a collection variable, so the Get a booking request can use `{{bookingId}}`. The second test checks speed, which is crude but catches a request that suddenly takes seconds. Send Book a room twice and the second run fails the first test with a 409, which is right: the room is taken. A collection that changes data needs a fresh test database, the next lesson's topic.

steps.title: OpenAPI: what's in a spec
steps.body:
Documentation written by hand drifts. Someone adds a field and forgets the docs, and a month later the docs describe an API that no longer exists. And prose can't be checked: a program can't read "send the room id and the times" and tell whether a request matches. Callers need a description precise enough for a program to read, and you need one you can check against what the API really does.

## What OpenAPI is

The **OpenAPI Specification** is a standard format for describing an HTTP API: every path and method, every parameter and body, every response with its status code and shape, and how callers authenticate. A description written in it is called an OpenAPI document, or a **spec**, and it's a file, in JSON or in YAML. It began in 2011 as Swagger, was renamed OpenAPI in 2016, and is now run by the OpenAPI Initiative. Version 3.1, from 2021, is what most tools read today, and 3.2, from 2025, adds a few features that tools are still catching up with. You'll still see the old name in tools like Swagger UI, and "Swagger 2.0" means the old format.

**YAML** is a way of writing the same data as JSON with less punctuation. Each line is `key: value`, nesting is shown by indentation instead of braces, a list item starts with `- `, and quotes are only needed when a value could be misread, like `"201"`, which would otherwise be a number. YAML is easier to write by hand, so hand-written specs use it, and tools that generate specs usually write JSON.

## The parts of a spec

The first example is a slice of Roombook's spec: the `POST /v1/bookings` operation and the pieces it uses. From the top:

- `openapi` is the version of the format, and `info` names the API and its own version, which goes up with each release.
- `servers` lists base URLs, so docs pages and tools know where to send requests.
- `paths` holds the endpoints. Under each path sit its methods, each one an **operation** with an `operationId`, a unique name that code generators turn into a function name like `createBooking`.
- `requestBody` and `responses` describe what goes in and what comes back, per status code and per media type. Roombook's errors are listed under `application/problem+json`, which is what the server really sends.
- `components` holds reusable pieces, and `$ref` points at them. `"#/components/schemas/Booking"` means the `Booking` schema further down this same file, so each shape is written once and used everywhere.
- `securitySchemes` says how to authenticate, here a bearer token, and `security` on the operation says this one needs it.

The schemas are **JSON Schema**, a standard language for describing JSON: `type`, `required`, `minimum`, `maxLength`, `format: date-time`, and `additionalProperties: false`, which rejects unknown fields. They mirror the validation you wrote in the validation lesson, and in Spring Boot you'll often generate one from the other, as the next part shows.

## What tools do with a spec

One file feeds a whole toolbox:

```diagram clients-and-openapi-spec-uses
One spec, read by many tools. Each stays right as long as the spec is.
```

- **Docs pages.** Swagger UI, Redoc, and Scalar turn the spec into a browsable reference with a Try it button that sends real requests.
- **Client code.** Generators read the spec and write typed clients in TypeScript, Python, Java, Go, and more, so callers get an SDK for free.
- **Mock servers.** Tools like Prism answer requests with the examples in the spec, so a mobile team can build against the API before it exists.
- **Tests.** Contract testing tools send requests built from the spec and check that each answer matches it. The next lesson runs one.
- **Linters.** Spectral and Redocly check the spec itself against style rules, like "every operation has a summary".
- **Postman**, from the previous part, imports it as a collection, and AI assistants and agents read it to learn how to call the API.

## What a spec can't say

A schema can say `startsAt` is a date-time. It can't say "on the hour or half past", "at most 14 days ahead", or "Ada can't hold more than three upcoming bookings". Rules like those go in `description` text for humans, and stay in your service code and your tests. That gap is real, and the next lesson shows a contract-testing tool tripping over it.

examples.title: Roombook's POST /v1/bookings, as OpenAPI
examples.prompt: A slice of the spec, in YAML: the booking operation, its body schema, and its security scheme. The full spec lists every endpoint the same way.
examples.code:
openapi: 3.1.1
info:
  title: Roombook API
  version: 1.4.0
servers:
  - url: https://api.roombook.example
  - url: http://localhost:8080
paths:
  /v1/bookings:
    post:
      operationId: createBooking
      summary: Book a room
      security:
        - bearerAuth: []
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: "#/components/schemas/CreateBookingRequest"
      responses:
        "201":
          description: The new booking
          headers:
            Location:
              schema:
                type: string
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Booking"
        "409":
          description: The room is already booked then
          content:
            application/problem+json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Problem"
        "422":
          description: A field breaks a booking rule
          content:
            application/problem+json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Problem"
components:
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth:
      type: http
      scheme: bearer
      bearerFormat: JWT
  schemas:
    CreateBookingRequest:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [roomId, startsAt, endsAt, attendees]
      properties:
        roomId:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
        startsAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time
          description: On the hour or half past, at most 14 days ahead.
        endsAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time
        attendees:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
          maximum: 30
        note:
          type: string
          maxLength: 500
examples.explanation: Read it from `paths` down: one operation, `createBooking`, which needs the bearer scheme and a JSON body matching `CreateBookingRequest`. It answers 201 with a `Booking` and a `Location` header, or a problem for 409 and 422, the codes the validation lesson chose. `CreateBookingRequest` holds the shape rules: four required fields, integers with minimums, date-time strings, and no extra fields. The `description` on `startsAt` carries a rule the schema can't express. `Booking` and `Problem`, cut from this slice, sit beside `CreateBookingRequest` under `components.schemas` in the same way.

steps.title: The spec in Spring Boot
steps.body:
There are two ways to keep a spec and the code in step, and every team picks one. **Code-first** means you write the routes and schemas in code and a tool generates the spec from them, so the spec can't forget an endpoint. **Spec-first** means you write the spec by hand, review it like code, and generate code from it or check the code against it, so the contract is designed before anyone writes a handler.

```diagram clients-and-openapi-code-first
Code-first derives the spec from the code. Spec-first derives the code, or its checks, from the spec.
```

Spring Boot doesn't make a spec by itself. **springdoc-openapi** does, code-first: add one dependency and it scans your controllers at startup and builds the spec from their mappings, parameters, and records.

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
  <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
  <version>3.2.1</version>
</dependency>
```

Version 3 is the line for Spring Boot 4. Restart, and the spec is at `/v3/api-docs` and Swagger UI at `/swagger-ui.html`. Spring Security blocks both until you add them to the `permitAll()` matchers, the same way as `/v1/auth/token`.

## What springdoc guesses, and what you tell it

springdoc reads your validation annotations, so `@NotNull`, `@Min(1)`, `@Max(30)`, and `@Size(max = 500)` on `CreateBookingRequest` become `required`, `minimum`, `maximum`, and `maxLength`. It can't see everything:

- A method returning `ResponseEntity<BookingView>` looks like a 200 to it, even though the code answers 201, and the errors your `@RestControllerAdvice` sends aren't listed at all.
- Without a declared media type it files responses under `*/*`. Setting `springdoc.default-produces-media-type` to `application/json` in `application.yaml` fixes that for the whole app.
- Security comes from annotations: `@SecurityScheme(name = "bearerAuth", type = HTTP, scheme = "bearer")` on a config class, and `@SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth")` on `BookingController`.

You fill in the rest with the Swagger annotations springdoc reads: `@Operation(summary = "Book a room")`, and an `@ApiResponse` for each status. Writing the Problem Details content on every error response gets long, so Roombook defines its own annotation, `@ProblemResponse`, that carries it, as the first example shows. `@Tag(name = "bookings")` groups operations in the docs, and `@Operation(deprecated = true)` marks one as deprecated.

## Checks in CI

The springdoc Maven plugin, `springdoc-openapi-maven-plugin`, starts the app during the build, downloads `/v3/api-docs` into `target/openapi.json`, and stops it. Commit that file and have CI compare it, `git diff --exit-code openapi.json`, so a change to the API shows up in the pull request. Lint it with `npx @redocly/cli lint openapi.json`. Callers generate typed clients from the same file, with openapi-generator for Java, or any generator for theirs.

examples.title: Documenting the booking operation
examples.prompt: `BookingController.create`, with the annotations springdoc reads, and `common/ProblemResponse.java`, Roombook's own annotation for error responses.
examples.explanation: `@ApiResponse(responseCode = "201")` corrects springdoc's guess of 200 and documents the `Location` header. `@ProblemResponse` is a **meta-annotation**: an annotation that carries another one, here an `@ApiResponse` whose content is `application/problem+json` with Spring's `ProblemDetail` as the schema. `@AliasFor` passes the code and description through, and `@Repeatable`, with a small `ProblemResponses` holder annotation, lets you stack several. springdoc understands Spring's meta-annotations, so each line becomes a full error response in the spec.

examples.title: What the spec says about booking
examples.prompt: With Roombook running on port 8080, ask springdoc's spec for each booking response's media types, then the body schema's rules.
examples.code:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs | jq '.paths["/v1/bookings"].post.responses | map_values(.content // {} | keys)'
curl -s http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs | jq '.components.schemas.CreateBookingRequest | {required, attendees: .properties.attendees}'
examples.explanation: The responses are the ones the annotations declared: 201 as JSON, and each error as `application/problem+json`. Their order in the output follows the order springdoc stored them, which doesn't matter to any tool. The schema came from the record and its constraints: the four `@NotNull` fields became `required`, sorted, and `@Min(1)` and `@Max(30)` on an `Integer` became an `int32` integer with bounds. The note is missing from `required` because it has no `@NotNull`.

steps.title: Changing an API without breaking callers
steps.body:
Once someone calls your API, you've made them a promise. A mobile app in the store can't be updated overnight, since some people never update. A partner's integration was written once, by someone who has moved on. If you rename a field on Tuesday, their code breaks on Tuesday, and they find out from their users. So the rule is: change the API by adding, and when you must break something, do it on purpose, slowly, and loudly.

## Safe changes and breaking ones

A change is **additive**, and safe, when every request that worked before still works and gets an answer old code can still read:

- a new endpoint, or a new method on an existing path
- a new optional request field, or a new optional query parameter
- a new field in a response
- a new error type for a new situation

A change is **breaking** when some existing caller can fail:

- removing or renaming a field, an endpoint, or a parameter
- changing a field's type, like an id from a number to a string
- making an optional field required, or adding a required one
- tightening validation, so a request that passed now gets a 422
- changing what a status code means, or which one you send
- adding a value to an enum that clients switch on, since code that handles "confirmed" and "cancelled" may crash on "pending"

New response fields are only safe if clients ignore fields they don't know. That habit is called being a **tolerant reader**, and Roombook's docs ask for it. Your own clients should practice it too.

## Versions

When you need a breaking change, you publish a new **version** and keep the old one running for a while. Roombook puts the version in the path, `/v1/bookings`, which is the most common choice: it's visible in every log line and every curl, and caches and gateways can route on it. Other APIs put it in a header, like `API-Version: 2`, or in the media type, `Accept: application/vnd.roombook.v2+json`. Those keep URLs stable but are easy to forget and hard to see.

Make a new version rarely. A version is a whole API you maintain twice, so most changes should be additive and stay in v1. Batch the breaking ones into one v2 with a clear reason.

Spring Framework 7 has API versioning built in. You configure where the version comes from in a `WebMvcConfigurer`, with `configureApiVersioning`: a path segment, a header like `API-Version`, a query parameter, or the media type. Then each mapping says which versions it serves, as in `@GetMapping(path = "/{id}", version = "2")`. The same configurer takes a deprecation handler that adds `Deprecation`, `Sunset`, and `Link` headers to every response from a version you've retired. Roombook's paths spell `/v1` out literally, so its v2 controllers would sit beside the v1 ones under `/v2`.

## Saying goodbye: Deprecation and Sunset

To retire something, tell callers in three ways: the docs and changelog, an email to everyone using it, and the responses themselves. Two standard headers do the last part. **Deprecation** says this is deprecated, from a date written as `@` and the time in seconds since 1970. **Sunset** says when it will stop working, as an HTTP date. A `Link` header points at the migration guide:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Deprecation: @1798761600
Sunset: Wed, 30 Jun 2027 00:00:00 GMT
Link: <https://roombook.example/docs/migrate-to-v2>; rel="deprecation"
```

Here `@1798761600` is 1 January 2027. Tools and SDKs can warn developers when they see these headers, and you can count which callers still hit the old version before you turn it off.

```diagram clients-and-openapi-sunset
Retiring v1: ship v2, mark v1 deprecated, give a sunset date, then answer 410.
```

After the sunset, the old endpoints answer `410 Gone` with a problem that points at the new version, rather than vanishing into 404s.

## Catching breaking changes before they ship

Nobody reviews every line of a big pull request for breaking changes. A tool can: **oasdiff** compares two versions of a spec and lists what changed, sorted by how dangerous it is. In CI, compare the spec on the main branch with the one in the pull request, and fail the build on any breaking change that isn't a planned version. The example shows it catching a renamed field and a new required one.

A spec, a collection, and oasdiff all check the API from the outside, one request at a time. The next lesson, Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Tests, checks it from the inside too, with tests that run on every change.

examples.title: oasdiff finds the breaking changes
examples.prompt: `openapi-main.yaml` is the spec on the main branch, and `openapi.yaml` the one in a pull request that renames the booking's `note` to `notes`, adds a required `purpose`, and adds a `building` filter to the room list.
examples.code:
oasdiff breaking openapi-main.yaml openapi.yaml --fail-on ERR
echo "exit code: $?"
examples.explanation: oasdiff found three breaking changes, each marked `error`. The new required `purpose` breaks every client that doesn't send it, and renaming `note` removes a field clients may read, on both operations that return a booking. It doesn't list the new `building` filter, since an optional parameter breaks nobody: `oasdiff changelog` lists that one too, as `info`. `--fail-on ERR` makes it exit with 1 when it finds an error, so CI stops the merge. Install it with `brew install oasdiff`, or run it in CI through its GitHub Action, `oasdiff/oasdiff-action`.
examples.output:
3 changes: 3 error, 0 warning, 0 info
error	[new-required-request-property] at openapi.yaml
	in API POST /v1/bookings
		added the new required request property `purpose`

error	[response-required-property-removed] at openapi-main.yaml
	in API POST /v1/bookings
		removed the required property `note` from the response with the `201` status

error	[response-required-property-removed] at openapi-main.yaml
	in API GET /v1/bookings/{bookingId}
		removed the required property `note` from the response with the `200` status


exit code: 1

recap:
- Callers only see requests, responses, and docs, so make every endpoint predictable and every error say what to fix.
- curl with `--json`, `-H`, `-i`, `-w`, and `--fail-with-body`, plus jq and a shell variable for the token, covers most API work in a terminal.
- Postman keeps shared collections of requests, with environments for each server, scripts that save tokens, and `pm.test` checks the CLI can run in CI.
- An OpenAPI document describes every path, body, response, and auth scheme in YAML or JSON, with JSON Schema for the shapes.
- One spec feeds docs pages, typed clients, mock servers, contract tests, and linters, but business rules still live in code and tests.
- Code-first generates the spec from the code, spec-first writes it by hand and checks the code against it, and either way CI checks the committed spec.
- Change an API by adding. Break it only in a new version, with Deprecation and Sunset headers, and let oasdiff catch accidental breaks.
